C0.quote: We study electoral competition between two win-motivated candidates
C0.note: Candidate-competition model with voters voting sincerely over two candidates (Downsian); borderline, but treated as eligible: strategic analysis of an electoral/voting procedure with voters' votes aggregated by majority.

C1.quote: we characterize the unique pure strategy equilibrium of the game

C2.1.value: votes (voters vote for the candidate giving highest utility)
C2.1.quote: voters vote for the candidate whose election would give them the highest utility

C2.2.quote: voters vote for the candidate whose election would give them the highest utility
C2.2.note: Vote for one of two candidates; binary choice, none of the listed formats.

C2.3.quote: Voters have a utility function with three components

C2.4.quote: voter i votes for candidate A if ui (A) > ui (B)
C2.4.note: Utilities (held) are separate from votes; footnote 6 says sincere voting is dominant, but the vote is modelled as a function of utility.

C3.1.quote: Since the behavior of the voters is unambiguous in this model
C3.1.note: Voters vote for preferred candidate; only candidates are strategic.

C3.2.quote: such a behavior is dominant even if there is a finite number of voters

C3.3.quote: such a behavior is dominant even if there is a finite number of voters
C3.3.note: Voting for the preferred option is dominant in a two-candidate election.

C4.1.note: Input is a vote between two candidates, not RANK/WEAK/APPR/DICH/PAIR; utilities directly defined.

C5.1.note: Results concern equilibrium platforms, polarization, expected policy outcome and win probabilities; no welfare or efficiency criteria evaluated.

VOT.quote_behav: voters vote for the candidate whose election would give them the highest utility
VOT.note: Voters take the voting action, fixed by the model.

CAN.quote_behav: Each candidate’s objective is to maximize his probability of winning the election.
CAN.quote_info: their reference policies are common information
CAN.note: Candidates choose platforms; they know each other's reference points and valence, but are uncertain about the median voter's ideal point (common prior).

OTH.note: Parties are discussed only outside the formal model.

C7.1.quote: Since the behavior of the voters is unambiguous in this model

C7.2.quote: such a behavior is dominant even if there is a finite number of voters
C7.2.note: Sincere voting is dominant for voters.

C8.1.quote: The solution concept we consider is Nash equilibrium.
C8.1.note: Also SPE mentioned for a sequential variant in Section 3.4.1, a side remark.

C8.2.quote: The solution concept we consider is Nash equilibrium.

claims.quote: novel insights regarding candidates’ flip-flopping incentives, and parties’ motives to nominate low-quality candidates
forces pushing parties to nominate lower-quality candidates are also present

C9.1.note: Claims about real institutions/party nomination behaviour.

C9.2.note: Claims about parties' policy-motivated nomination need an assumption that parties are policy-motivated and care about outcome; the nomination stage is not modelled (paper admits it does not model it). Needed assumptions are partly stated as caveats.
